title: Job's ending (Job 42)
hook: Job prays for his friends, and his daughters are named and given an inheritance

segments.voice: Yesterday, the voice from the whirlwind, asking where were you? What wild, huge thing did you look at, and how big did your worry feel next to it? Day four hundred forty-nine.

Jemima. Keziah. Keren-happuch. Three girls' names from the very last page of the book of Job. It's an odd place for names to come from: a book of loss, accusation and storm. But the ending of Job has surprises in it, and the daughters are one of them. Before we get to them, though, the story has unfinished business. Job has seen God. The friends who explained his pain are still standing there. And God has something to say to them.
screen: `JEMIMA, KEZIAH, KEREN-HAPPUCH.` → `THE LAST PAGE OF JOB.` → `UNFINISHED BUSINESS.`

segments.voice: First, Job answers the whirlwind. In the King James Bible: "I have heard of thee by the hearing of the ear: but now mine eye seeth thee." He doesn't get an explanation. He gets an encounter, and it's enough to quiet him. Then the book switches back to prose, and God turns to Eliphaz: "My wrath is kindled against thee, and against thy two friends: for ye have not spoken of me the thing that is right, as my servant Job hath." Read that twice. Job, who cursed his birthday and argued with God for chapters, spoke rightly. The friends, who defended God with tidy rules, did not. Honest complaint, the book suggests, is closer to the truth than a neat explanation. But here's the turn. The friends must bring an offering, and Job must pray for them. The men who hurt him. "And the LORD turned the captivity of Job, when he prayed for his friends: also the LORD gave Job twice as much as he had before." When he prayed for his friends. That's where the healing turns. Then the family. Job has seven sons and three daughters again. The sons aren't named. The daughters are: Jemima, Keziah and Keren-happuch, names that some readers take to mean dove, cassia, a fragrant spice, and a horn of eye paint. And their father "gave them inheritance among their brethren." In the law in Numbers, daughters inherit when there are no sons; here they inherit alongside their brothers. Some readers are uneasy that new children are counted as restoration, and the book doesn't say the grief was erased. It ends simply: Job died, "being old and full of days."
screen: `NOW MINE EYE SEETH THEE` · `YE HAVE NOT SPOKEN RIGHT` · `WHEN HE PRAYED FOR HIS FRIENDS` · `DAUGHTERS NAMED, AND INHERITING` · then, large: `OLD AND FULL OF DAYS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: wish good to someone who hurt you. This one is hard, so go gently. Sit, and let your breath slow. Bring to mind someone who wounded you. If the deepest wound is too much today, choose someone who hurt you a little: a sharp word, a careless friend. You don't have to excuse what they did. Job didn't. Just hold them in mind. If you pray, you can ask God's good for them, simply, even through clenched teeth. If you don't pray, try wishing them well for one breath, then another. The bell holds the time.
Job's ending. Job sees God, prays for the friends who hurt him, and gives his named daughters an inheritance.
Your line: pray for the friends. Today, when that person comes to mind, wish them one good thing instead of replaying the hurt. Day four hundred forty-nine.

howItsDone: Following Jesus's command to pray for those who wrong them, many Christians include people who have hurt them in their daily prayers, and Job's prayer for his friends is often cited as an example.

original.note: Hebrew: Jemima, Job's first daughter. the name is often taken to mean dove.

trapdoor: what you thought: a happy ending where Job gets everything back double.

what a scholar hears: the names are often read as dove, cassia and a horn of eye paint; in Numbers 27 daughters inherit only when there are no sons.

Daughters' inheritance: in Numbers 27 daughters inherit when there are no sons; Job's daughters inherit alongside brothers. Confirm 'rare'.
